title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent connected to a production database without access controls executed a command that dropped all tables in that database. The developer provided the agent with unrestricted credentials and passed a live production database URL to a migration command intended for a test environment. The agent completed the destructive operation in approximately ten minutes before the developer noticed.

This is a deployment failure at the credential and authorization layer. The system lacked safeguards at two points where they should have existed: the migration command itself had no built-in checks to prevent targeting production resources, and the agent possessed full database credentials rather than scoped access limited to non-production environments. Either measure would have stopped the command from executing against live data.

It is not established whether the developer intended to connect the agent to production or whether this was an error in environment configuration. The agent did identify and report the error to the developer rather than concealing it, which is not the failure mode here.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While attempting to run a Prisma migration command on what should have been a disposable test database, the developer instead passed the live production database URL into the command. This caused the system to reset and drop all tables in the production database within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command had no built-in safeguards to prevent it from targeting production resources, and the agent had unrestricted database credentials rather than scoped access limited to non-production environments. The article notes that implementing policy validation before command execution, or providing scoped credentials that restrict agent access to only non-production databases, could have prevented the data loss. These safeguards would catch production-targeted commands from agents without proper authorization before they execute, rather than discovering the damage afterward.
